## Introduction

### Overview

In Exercises 1--5, you'll continue exploring the RNA-seq results from
[this week's lecture](w15a_rnaseq.qmd).
In Exercise 6, you'll turn your analysis into a polished Quarto report,
practicing with the Quarto material from
[week 14](../week14/w14a_quarto.qmd).

::: callout-tip
#### Lecture page exercises
Make sure to do any of the exercises on this week's lecture page that we did
not do in class.
Also, if you struggled with any of the exercises we did do in class,
go over those again.
:::

### Setting up

1. Start an RStudio session at OSC and open your RStudio Project
   ([Starting an RStudio Server session at OSC](../week12/w12a_r-basics.qmd#starting-an-rstudio-server-session-at-osc)).

2. Create a new Quarto document `w15_exercises.qmd` in your `week15` folder,
   with a YAML header with a title, your name, the date, and `embed-resources: true`
   ([Creating a Quarto document](../week12/w12a_r-basics.qmd#creating-a-quarto-document)).

3. These exercises build on the DESeq2 object that you saved at the end of the lecture
   ([Exporting the results](w15a_rnaseq.qmd#exporting-the-results)).
   If you didn't run that code yet, do so in your lecture document first.
   Then, add the following chunk to the top of your exercises document,
   which will load the packages and recreate the objects from the lecture that you'll need:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(DESeq2)
library(EnhancedVolcano)
library(pheatmap)

# Load the DESeq2 object that you saved in the lecture
dds <- readRDS("results/DE/dds.rds")

# Recreate some other objects from the lecture
meta <- as.data.frame(colData(dds))
count_mat <- counts(dds)
dds_vst <- varianceStabilizingTransformation(dds)
res_rc24 <- results(dds, contrast = c("group", "relictum_24hpi", "control_24hpi"))
```
:::



::: {.cell}

:::


## Exercise 1: Gene counts and library sizes

1. How many genes have *mean* counts (across all samples) of at least 10?

2. In the lecture, we computed the "library sizes" (summed gene counts per sample)
   with `colSums(count_mat)`.
   That output is not so easy to read or interpret.
   Instead, get these numbers in millions, rounded to whole numbers,
   and sorted from low to high.

## Exercise 2: Volcano plots and outliers

The `EnhancedVolcano()` function by default adds gene IDs to highly significant genes,
but in the lecture, we turned off gene name labeling by setting `labSize = 0`.
This is because the default p-value cut-off for point labeling is `1e-5`, and in this case,
that would make the plot quite busy with gene labels.

1. Play around with the p-value cut-off and the labeling to create a volcano plot you like.
   Check [the vignette](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/EnhancedVolcano/inst/doc/EnhancedVolcano.html),
   or the help page (`?EnhancedVolcano`) to see how you can do this.

2. In the volcano plot, one gene stands out with a very high log2-fold change.
   Figure out the identity of this gene,
   either by labeling it in the plot, or by filtering the `res_rc24` table.

3. Plot the expression levels of this gene across treatments and time points,
   like we did for the top DEG in the lecture
   ([Plot specific genes](w15a_rnaseq.qmd#plot-specific-genes)).
   How would you interpret this?

## Exercise 3: A customized PCA plot

1. Compare the PCA plot with different numbers of included genes.
   (Hint: figure out how to do so by looking at the help by running `?plotPCA`.)

2. Customize the PCA plot: can you "separate" treatment and time point
   (different shapes for one variable, and different colors for the other),
   like in Fig. 1 of the paper?

<details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for some hints for PCA plot customization_</summary>

In the plot we made in the lecture, each combination of
time point and treatment has a distinct color --- it would be better to use **point
color** only to distinguish one of the variables, and **point shape** to distinguish the
other variable (as was also done in the paper's Fig. 1).

To be able to customize the plot properly, we best build it from scratch ourselves, rather
than using the `plotPCA` function. But then how do we get the input data in the right
shape?

A nice trick is that we can use `returnData = TRUE` in the `plotPCA` function, to get
plot-ready formatted data instead of an actual plot:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pca_df <- plotPCA(
  dds_vst,
  ntop = 500,
  intgroup = c("time", "treatment"),
  returnData = TRUE
)
```
:::


With that `pca_df` dataframe in hand,
it will be relatively straightforward to customize the plot using your knowledge
of ggplot2.

</details>

## Exercise 4: More DEGs

1. The paper's Table 1 also reports the number of DEGs with an **absolute LFC \> 1**.
   Find out how many up- and downregulated DEGs with an absolute LFC \> 1
   we have for the `relictum_24hpi` vs. `control_24hpi` comparison.

2. Extract the results for one or more **other contrasts** in the paper's Table 1,
   and compare the numbers of DEGs with those in the table.

## Exercise 5: Heatmaps

1. Make a heatmap with the top-25 **most highly expressed** genes
   (i.e., genes with the highest mean expression levels across all samples).

<details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for a hint: how to get that top-25_</summary>


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
norm_mat <- assay(dds_vst)
top25_hi <- names(sort(rowMeans(norm_mat), decreasing = TRUE)[1:25])
```
:::


</details>

## Exercise 6: A polished Quarto report

Use the Quarto material from [week 14](../week14/w14a_quarto.qmd) to turn
your `w15_exercises.qmd` into a nicely formatted report.

1. Add the following to your YAML header:
   a table of contents, a theme of your choice,
   and `execute` options that hide all warnings and messages in the document.

2. Add a header for each exercise,
   and a sentence or two of Markdown text above or below each plot that describes what it shows.

3. Hide the code (but not the output) of the setup chunk at the top of your document
   with a chunk option.

4. Give your volcano plot from Exercise 2 a figure caption and a custom width and height
   ([Figure options in Quarto documents](../week13/w13b_data-viz.qmd#figure-options-in-quarto-documents)).

5. In your text, report the number of DEGs for the `relictum_24hpi` vs. `control_24hpi`
   comparison using **inline code**, so the number is computed when you render the document.

6. Render the document and check that everything looks the way you intended.

## Solutions

### Exercise 1

<details><summary>**1.** Genes with mean counts of at least 10</summary>

We need to divide the row sums by the number of samples, which is the number of columns,
which we can get with `ncol()`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nrow(count_mat[rowSums(count_mat) / ncol(count_mat) >= 10, ])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output
[1] 12529
```


:::
:::


Alternatively, you can use the `rowMeans()` function:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nrow(count_mat[rowMeans(count_mat) >= 10, ])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output
[1] 12529
```


:::
:::


</details>

<details><summary>**2.** Library sizes in millions</summary>


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sort(round(colSums(count_mat) / 1000000))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output

          9          15          17          18          18          19 
ERR10802882 ERR10802884 ERR10802867 ERR10802879 ERR10802883 ERR10802874

ERR10802865 ERR10802880 ERR10802863 ERR10802869 ERR10802885 ERR10802870 
         23          23          24          24          24          25 
ERR10802886 ERR10802866 ERR10802871 ERR10802876 
         25          27          27          29 
```

</details>

### Exercise 2

<details><summary>**1.** A volcano plot with gene labels</summary>


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
EnhancedVolcano(
  toptable = res_rc24,
  title = "relictum vs. control at 24 hpi",
  x = "log2FoldChange",
  y = "padj",
  lab = rownames(res_rc24),
  labSize = 4, # Now we will show the gene labels
  pCutoff = 10e-10, # Modify the p-value cut-off
  subtitle = NULL, # I'll also remove the silly subtitle
  caption = NULL, # ... and the caption
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

``` warning-r-output
Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.
ℹ The deprecated feature was likely used in the EnhancedVolcano package.
  Please report the issue to the authors.
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

``` warning-r-output
Warning: The `size` argument of `element_line()` is deprecated as of ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use the `linewidth` argument instead.
ℹ The deprecated feature was likely used in the EnhancedVolcano package.
  Please report the issue to the authors.
```


:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


</details>

<details><summary>**2.** The identity of the log2-fold change outlier</summary>

- Labeling it in the plot:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
EnhancedVolcano(
  toptable = res_rc24,
  title = "relictum vs. control at 24 hpi",
  x = "log2FoldChange",
  y = "padj",
  lab = rownames(res_rc24),
  labSize = 4,
  pCutoff = 0.05, # Modify the p-value cut-off
  FCcutoff = 20, # Modify the LFC cut-off
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

``` warning-r-output
Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_vline()`).
```


:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


- Finding it in the results table:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
as.data.frame(res_rc24) |> filter(log2FoldChange > 20)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output
              baseMean log2FoldChange    lfcSE     stat       pvalue
LOC120413430  7.540043       24.46898 5.397990 4.532979           NA
LOC120431476 39.720375       23.01445 5.301369 4.341228 1.416885e-05
                     padj
LOC120413430           NA
LOC120431476 0.0008584396
```


:::
:::


(Interestingly, there's a second gene with a LFC \> 20 that we hadn't seen in the plot,
because it has `NA` as the `pvalue` and `padj`.
See the collapsed box "`NA` values in the DESeq2 results table" in the lecture
for why p-values can be set to `NA`.)

</details>

<details><summary>**3.** Plot the outlier gene</summary>


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
focal_gene_counts <- plotCounts(
  dds,
  gene = "LOC120431476",
  intgroup = c("time", "treatment"),
  returnData = TRUE
)

focal_gene_counts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = count, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point(size = 4, shape = 21, position = position_jitter(w = 0.1, h = 0)) +
  facet_wrap(vars(time)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Wow! It looks like in every single time + treatment combination, all but one (or in one
case, two) of the samples have zero expression, but there are several extreme outliers.

For our focal comparison at `24hpi` (left panel/facet), comparing `control` vs `relictum`,
it looks like the difference between these two groups is solely due to the one outlier
in `relictum`. Nevertheless, even the multiple-testing corrected p-value (`padj`) is
significant for this gene:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
as.data.frame(res_rc24) |>
  rownames_to_column("gene") |>
  filter(gene == "LOC120431476")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output
          gene baseMean log2FoldChange    lfcSE     stat       pvalue
1 LOC120431476 39.72038       23.01445 5.301369 4.341228 1.416885e-05
          padj
1 0.0008584396
```


:::
:::


So, we have to be careful with taking our statistical results at face value, and need to
visualize important genes!

</details>

### Exercise 3

<details><summary>**1.** PCA with different numbers of genes</summary>

The `ntop` argument sets the number of genes (with the highest variance) to use,
which is 500 by default:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plotPCA(dds_vst, ntop = 100, intgroup = c("time", "treatment"))
plotPCA(dds_vst, ntop = 5000, intgroup = c("time", "treatment"))
```
:::


</details>

<details><summary>**2.** A customized PCA plot</summary>

First, get the data in the right format, as explained in the hint:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pca_df <- plotPCA(
  dds_vst,
  ntop = 500,
  intgroup = c("time", "treatment"),
  returnData = TRUE
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

``` regular-r-output
using ntop=500 top features by variance
```


:::
:::


Second, extract and store the percentage of variance explained by different
principal components, so you can later add this information to the plot:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pct_var <- round(100 * attr(pca_df, "percentVar"), 1)
pct_var
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output
[1] 85.3  3.1
```


:::
:::


Now we can make the plot:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pca_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = treatment, shape = time)) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PC1 (", pct_var[1], "%)"),
    y = paste0("PC2 (", pct_var[2], "%)")
  ) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = "Infection status") +
  scale_shape(name = "Time points") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


</details>

### Exercise 4

<details><summary>**1.** DEGs with an absolute LFC \> 1</summary>

- **Solution using tidyverse/dplyr:**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# First we need to convert the results table into a regular data frame
as.data.frame(res_rc24) |>
  # Then we only select the rows/genes that are significant
  filter(padj < 0.05, abs(log2FoldChange) > 1) |>
  # If we run count() on a logical test, we get the nrs. that are FALSE v. TRUE
  dplyr::count(log2FoldChange > 0)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output
  log2FoldChange > 0   n
1              FALSE 159
2               TRUE  49
```


:::
:::


- **Solution using base R:**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Down-regulated (relictum < control):
sum(res_rc24$log2FoldChange < -1 & res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output
[1] 159
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Up-regulated (relictum > control):
sum(res_rc24$log2FoldChange > 1 & res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output
[1] 49
```


:::
:::


</details>

<details><summary>**2.** Other contrasts</summary>

For example, for `cathemerium` vs. `control` at 24 hpi:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
res_cc24 <- results(dds, contrast = c("group", "cathemerium_24hpi", "control_24hpi"))
sum(res_cc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output
[1] 236
```


:::
:::


</details>

### Exercise 5

<details><summary>**1.** A heatmap of the most highly expressed genes</summary>


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# In the normalized count matrix, select only the genes of interest
norm_mat_sel <- norm_mat[match(top25_hi, rownames(norm_mat)), ]

# Sort the metadata
meta_sort <- meta |>
  arrange(treatment, time) |>
  select(treatment, time)

# Create the heatmap
pheatmap(
  norm_mat_sel,
  annotation_col = meta_sort,
  cluster_cols = FALSE,
  show_rownames = FALSE,
  scale = "row"
)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


</details>
